# Two-Sample t-Test

> This lab is adapted from Kevin P. McIntyre's [OSL Open Stats Lab](https://sites.google.com/view/openstatslab/home/regression-activities?pli=1&authuser=0).

We will continue to explore the data from @tworek_why_2016, where they investigated people's bias to prefer explanations that are based on inherent properties over extrinsic explanations.

## Paired Samples t-Test

In the previous lab, we conducted a one-sample t-test to see if there was a difference in endorsement of inherent vs. extrinsic explanations. The same participants were asked to rate their agreement with both types of explanations, so the data are paired. One-sample t-test and Paired-samples t-test are equivalent, and this time, we will conduct the same analysis using a paired-samples t-test.

### Null Hypothesis and Alternative Hypothesis

The null hypothesis is that the average endorsement is the same for inherent and extrinsic explanations. The alternative hypothesis is that the average endorsement is different for inherent and extrinsic explanations.

$$H_0: \mu_\text{inherent} = \mu_\text{extrinsic}$$
$$H_1: \mu_\text{inherent} \neq \mu_\text{extrinsic}$$

Put differently, 

$$H_0: \mu_\text{Diff} = 0$$
$$H_1: \mu_\text{Diff} \neq 0$$

### Data

```{r}
df <- read_csv('data/tworek2016_study2.csv') %>%
  as_tibble() %>%
  select(diff, ihav, extav, excluded) %>% 
  filter(excluded == 0)
glimpse(df)
```

```{r}
describe(df) %>%
  knitr::kable() 
```

### Check Assumptions

### Normality

```{r}
df %>% 
    ggplot(aes(x = diff)) +
    geom_histogram(bins = 20, color = "black", fill = "lightblue") +
    labs(x = "Inherence Bias", y = "Frequency") +
    theme_classic()
```

### t-test

```{r}
res_onesample_t <- t.test(df$diff,
                mu = 0, 
                alternative = "two.sided")
res_onesample_t
```

```{r}
res_paired_t <- t.test(df$ihav, df$extav,
                paired = TRUE,
                alternative = "two.sided")
res_paired_t
```

You can see that the results are identical, because whether the two means are the same is the same thing as asking whether the mean of the difference scores is 0. 

### Read in and clean the data 

#### Select the variables of interest

We can select these variables using the `select()` function from the `dplyr` package. The output of `select()` is a new data frame that contains only the variables we selected, and will be used for our analysis in `df`.

```{r}
df <- read_csv('data/tworek2016_study4.csv') %>%
  as_tibble() %>%
  select(Excluded, InherenceBias, Condition, Gender) %>%
  mutate(Condition = factor(Condition, levels = c("Anti-Inherence", "Control"))) %>%
  mutate(Gender = factor(Gender, levels = c("Woman", "Man", "Other")))
```


#### Inspect the variables as rows: `glimpse()` from `tidyverse`

```{r}
glimpse(df)
```


#### Remove excluded participants

There are 131 observations in this dataset, but we know some particpants were excluded from the analysis. Let's check how many participants were excluded.

```{r}
df %>%
  tabyl(Excluded) %>%
  adorn_totals("row") %>%
  adorn_pct_formatting(digits = 2) %>% 
  knitr::kable()
```

Excluded participants are marked with 1 in the `Excluded` variable. We can filter out these participants using the `filter()` function from the `dplyr` package. The output of `filter()` is a new data frame that contains only the rows that meet the condition we specified, and will be used for our analysis in `df`.

```{r}
df <- df %>%
  filter(Excluded == 0)
```

Now check the number of observations in the dataset again. It should be 122.

```{r}
glimpse(df)
```

### Inspect the Data

#### Summary Statistics: `describe()` from the `psych` package

```{r}
describe(df) %>%
  knitr::kable() 
```

## Check Assumptions

There are three assumptions for a one-sample t-test. Two of those are more about the design: (1) the data are continuous (interval or ratio scale) and (2) the data are independent -- no same participant is measured more than once in our sample. The data is indeed continuous, because it is the average of 15 items that are measured on a 9-point scale. We will assume that the authors took care to ensure that the data are independent. 

### Normality

The third assumption is about the distribution of the data: (3) the data are normally distributed. t-test is robust to moderate violations of normality, but we will still check the distribution of the data using a histogram and the Shapiro-Wilk test.

```{r}
df %>% 
    ggplot(aes(x = InherenceBias)) +
    facet_wrap(~Condition) +
    geom_histogram(bins = 9, color = "black", fill = "lightblue") +
    labs(x = "Inherence Bias", y = "Frequency") +
    theme_classic()
```

#### Shapiro-Wilk Test: `shapiro.test()` from base R

There is a statistical test for normality called the Shapiro-Wilk test. The null hypothesis for the Shapiro-Wilk test is that the data are normally distributed. If the p-value is less than 0.05, we reject the null hypothesis and conclude that the data are not normally distributed. So here, what we are looking for is that "there is not enough evidence that the data are not normally distributed" -- when p > .05, we proceed with the test.

:::{.callout-caution}
##### Help! My Shapiro-Wilk Test p-value is less than 0.05!

You can breathe. t-test is robust to moderate violations of normality, and the Shapiro-Wilk test is very sensitive when the sample size is large. When the sample size is large, even small deviations from normality can lead to a significant result. Therefore, it is important to also look at the histogram of the data to see if the distribution is approximately normal. Even if the p-value is less than .05, if your histogram is not too skewed or too heavy-tailed, you can still proceed with the t-test. 

If your sample size is small and the p-value is less than .05, you may want to consider using a non-parametric test instead of the t-test. Non-parametric tests do not assume normality, but they are less powerful than parametric tests.

A non-parametric alternative to the one-sample t-test is the Wilcoxon signed-rank test -- instead of testing hypotheses about the mean, it tests hypotheses about the median (hence, the "rank"). You can use the `wilcox.test()` function from base R to conduct the Wilcoxon signed-rank test.
:::

```{r}
shapiro.test(df %>% filter(Condition == "Control") %>% pull(InherenceBias))
shapiro.test(df %>% filter(Condition == "Anti-Inherence") %>% pull(InherenceBias))
```

There is no evidence that the data are not normally distributed, so the assumption of normality is met, and we are good to go with the t-test.

### Homogeneity of Variance

```{r}
leveneTest(InherenceBias ~ Condition, data = df)
leveneTest(InherenceBias ~ Gender, data = df %>% filter(Gender != "Other"))
```

## Independent Samples t-Test

To compute the independent samples t-test, we will use the `t.test()` function from base R. The first argument is the variable we want to test, the second argument `mu` is the hypothesized population mean (5 in this case), and the third argument `alternative` is the alternative hypothesis ("two.sided" for a two-tailed t-test).

```{r}
t.test(InherenceBias ~ Condition, 
       data = df,
       var.equal = FALSE,
       alternative = "two.sided")
```

Let's unpack the output. 

In the first line, it reports the t statistic (test statistic t), the degrees of freedom (df), the p-value (p). 

t distribution's shape is determined by the degrees of freedom, so it is essential to report the degrees of freedom along with the t statistic and p-value.

> t(df) = t statistic, p = p-value

Because the p-value is very small, we can report it as p < .001. 

> $t(263.89) = -4.2919$, $p < .001$

If you just report this, however, you are depriving your readers of the information about what your sample estimate is, and how confident you can be about that estimate. The output also reports the sample mean (mean of x) and the 95% confidence interval for the population mean (95 percent confidence interval).

> M = sample mean, 95% CI [lower bound, upper bound]

In a sentence, it looks like this:

> The average inherence bias score was significantly reduced in the Anti-Inherence condition ($M_\text{Anti-Inherence} = 5.64$) than in the Control condition ($M_\text{Control} = 6.28$; $M_\text{diff}$ = -0.63), 95% CI $[-0.92, -0.34]$, $t(263.89) = -4.2919$, $p < .001$. 

There is an easy way to print this in the APA style using the `apa_print()` function from the `papaja` package. The output is a list of character strings that can be printed in the manuscript.

The probability of observing sample means as extreme as the one we observed or more extreme, given the baseline value of 5, is less than 0.05. Therefore, we can reject the null hypothesis and conclude that the average inherence bias score in the population is significantly different from 5. Because the average is greater than 5, we can report that there is a significant inherence bias in the population.


```{r}
res_apa <- t.test(InherenceBias ~ Condition, 
       data = df,
       var.equal = FALSE,
       alternative = "two.sided") %>%
    papaja::apa_print()
res_apa$full_result
```

You can print this in the Quarto document using the ``` `r` ``` inline code chunk.

```` r res_apa$full_result ````

`r res_apa$full_result`

### Effect Size (Cohen's d)

We will report the effect size using Cohen's d. We can compute it using the `cohensD()` function from the `lsr` package. `mu` is the hypothesized population mean at the baseline (the midpoint of the scale).

```{r}
d <- cohensD(InherenceBias ~ Condition, data = df, method = "unequal")
d
```

## Write up the results

> A independent-samples t-test was performed to compare inherence bias scores between the Anti-Inherence and Control conditions. The results indicated that the mean inherence bias was significantly lower in the Anti-Inherence condition, `r res_apa$full_result`, with a moderate effect size, d = `r round(d, 2)`. These results suggest that the priming extrinsic explanations can reduce inherence bias.

:::{.callout-tip}
## One-Sample t-Test Write-Up Checklist

- What type of test was performed, to test what hypothesis?
- Which DV was tested, and what was the baseline value it was compared to?
- What was your estimate of the mean?
  - M
  - 95% CI
- What are the results of the analysis? 
  - Was the mean significantly higher or lower than the baseline? In which direction?
  - t statistic
  - degrees of freedom
  - p-value
- What was the practical significance of the results?
  - Small, medium, or large effect size?
  - Cohen's d
- What does the statistical result mean in the context of the research question?
:::

You've completed a one-sample t-test! Woohoo!

## Exercise 1

:::{.callout-tip}
#### Study 2

Do you find the results from Study 1 convincing? For one, what if people just have a general tendency to agree with any statement, regardless of whether it is based on inherent or extrinsic properties? To address this concern, @tworek_why_2016 conducted a second study.

This time, the inherence bias score was measured as a relative preference for inherent explanations over extrinsic explanations for the same 15 items. For example, participants were presented with a statement like "Pink is the color associated with girls because of something about the color pink or about girls— maybe because pink's flower-like appearance matches girls' dainty nature" and asked to rate their agreement with that statement on a 9-point scale. Then, they were presented with a statement like "Pink is the color associated with girls because of some historical or contextual reason—maybe because businesses promoted pink products for girls over the last century." and asked to rate their agreement with that statement on a 9-point scale. The relative preference score is the difference between the two scores (inherent - extrinsic). This difference score is in `diff` variable in the dataset. The baseline value is 0, which indicates no preference for either type of explanation.

There are 139 participants in this study. 27 participants were excluded from the analysis (marked as 1 in the `excluded` variable), resulting in 112 participants in the final analysis.


**Repeat the one-sample t-test for study 2 in the `tworek2016_study2.csv` file.** Write up the results in APA style, interpreting the results in the context of the research question.
:::

### Bonus Exercise: Demographics Data and External Validity
Whenever you conduct a study, it is important to report the demographics of your sample. The demographics data is in the `Age` and `Gender` variables in Study 1, and `age` and `gender` variables in Study 2. 

Use the `tabyl()` function from the `janitor` package to create frequency tables for the demographics data. Do you find any interesting patterns in the demographics data? How might these patterns affect the generalizability of the results?
:::


:::{.callout-tip}
### Bonus Exercise: Reliability Analysis
They've used a 15-item scale to measure inherence bias. Using the reliability analysis we learned in lab 2, compute Cronbach's alpha for the 15 items. Report the results in APA style, interpreting the results in the context of the research question. 

In study 1, the variables start with `ih01`, `ih02`, ..., `ih15` in the dataset. The two attention check items are `ihc1` and `ihc2`, so you should exclude them from the analysis. You can combine `starts_with()` within `select()` to select the 15 desired items. The `Excluded` variable is also in the dataset, so you should use that variable to filter out participants who are excluded from the analysis. 

In study 2, the variables that are relevant for the reliability analysis are `ih01`, `ih02`, ..., `ih15` and `ext01`, `ext02`, ..., `ext15`. The two attention check items are `ihcatch1` and `ihcatch2`, so you should exclude them from the analysis. The average scores for each participant are in the `ihav` and `extav` variables, which should not be included in the reliability analysis, as they are already aggregated scores. 

Because the ih and ext items are measuring the opposite constructs, you should reverse -code the ext items before computing Cronbach's alpha. 

For study 2, the `excluded` variable is also in the dataset, so you should filter out participants who are excluded from the analysis as well.
:::
